description.en: The assisted hanging knee raise uses an assistance machine to scale the bodyweight load of a hanging knee raise. The lifter places the knees on the assist pad of a pull up machine, then raises the knees toward the chest. It is a beginner friendly hanging abs move.

en: Set up a pull up assist machine with a knee pad.
Set the assistance weight to scale the load.
Step onto the knee pad with both knees.
Grip the upper handles with both hands.
Hang from the bar with the knee pad supporting some bodyweight.
Brace your core hard.
Raise the knees up toward the chest by curling the pelvis.
Lower back down with control.
Beginner friendly abs move
Trains the rectus abdominis
Useful pull up progression
Builds the abs
Strong machine move
Easy to scale loading

description.en: The band-assisted dip loops a resistance band over parallel dip bars and under your knees to assist your dip by reducing your effective bodyweight. The thicker the band, the more assistance. It is the best regression for developing the strength to do unassisted dips.

en: Loop a thick resistance band over one dip bar handle. Pull the other end to the opposite bar to create a loop between them.
Grip the bars and place one or both knees in the band loop below you.
Start with arms locked out, body supported above the bars.
Lower your body by bending at the elbows until your upper arms are at least parallel to the floor.
The band assists you by pushing upward.
Press back up to lockout by extending your elbows.
Use progressively thinner bands as you get stronger.
Goal: work toward unassisted dips.
Best dip regression for strength development
Adjustable assistance with band thickness
Allows proper dip form while building strength
Builds chest, tricep, and shoulder strength
Natural movement path unlike machine-assisted
Inexpensive equipment

description.en: The band side triceps extension performs tricep extensions with the arm reaching out to the side using a band anchored at the same side. The lateral path of the extension targets the lateral head of the triceps differently than overhead or pulldown extensions. It is a strong choice for tricep variation.

en: Anchor a resistance band at chest height.
Stand sideways to the anchor with the right side closer.
Grip the band end with your right hand.
Bring your right elbow up to shoulder level out to the side.
Bend your right elbow to 90 degrees with hand near your face.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Extend the elbow to straighten the arm out to the side.
Squeeze the tricep at the lockout, then bend the elbow back. Switch sides.
Direct lateral tricep head emphasis
Different angle than standard extensions
Builds tricep size and detail
Constant band tension
No weights required
Useful for tricep variation

description.en: The barbell lying close grip press is performed lying on the floor with a close grip on the barbell. The floor stops the descent at the elbows, creating a partial range that emphasizes the triceps while protecting the shoulders. It is a strong tricep builder for lifters with shoulder issues.

en: Lie on the floor under a barbell set up on low rack pins or held by a partner.
Plant your feet flat on the floor with knees bent.
Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width or slightly closer.
Pull your shoulder blades back and brace your core.
Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar with control until your elbows touch the floor.
Pause briefly, then press the bar back up by extending the elbows.
Squeeze the triceps at the top.
Floor protects the shoulders
Builds tricep size and lockout strength
Partial range allows heavier loads
Useful for lifters with shoulder issues
Practical for home training
Strong tricep specialization

description.en: The barbell lying extension (skull crusher) is a tricep isolation exercise where you lie on a flat bench and lower a barbell toward your forehead by bending at the elbows, then extend back to lockout. It is one of the best exercises for building tricep mass with heavy loading.

en: Lie on a flat bench. Hold a barbell (or EZ bar) with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Press the bar up to lockout above your chest.
Keeping your upper arms vertical, bend at the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead.
Lower under control until the bar is just above or behind your forehead.
Extend your elbows to press the bar back up to lockout.
Squeeze your triceps at the top.
Keep your elbows pointing toward the ceiling — do not let them flare.
Use moderate weight and controlled tempo for safety.
Heavy tricep loading for mass building
Targets all three tricep heads
Allows progressive overload with a barbell
One of the most effective tricep exercises
Builds lockout strength for bench press
Simple setup

description.en: The barbell muscle snatch is a snatch variation where you pull the barbell from the floor (or hang) all the way overhead to lockout without dropping under the bar at all. There is no quarter squat or full squat catch — just a continuous strict pull all the way overhead. It is a technique developer for the upper-body pull and shoulder strength.

en: Set up with a barbell using a wide snatch grip. Bar at hang position (mid-thigh) or floor.
Brace your core. Set your back flat.
Begin the pull by hinging slightly and explosively extending your hips and knees.
As the bar passes your hips, shrug your shoulders aggressively.
Continue pulling the bar straight up, keeping it close to your body.
Pull the bar up past your face and continue until it locks out overhead.
Do NOT drop under the bar — your feet stay flat on the floor throughout.
Lower the bar with control and reset. Use much lighter weight than power snatches.
Builds upper-body pulling strength for the snatch
Trains shoulder mobility and strength
Excellent technique developer
Strict form eliminates the catch phase
Useful warm-up before heavier snatches
Builds trap and shoulder strength

description.en: The barbell reverse wrist curl is a forearm extensor exercise performed with an overhand (palms-down) grip on a barbell. You sit with forearms on a bench, wrists hanging off, and curl the bar upward by extending your wrists. It builds the top of the forearm and helps prevent tennis elbow.

en: Sit on a bench. Place your forearms flat on the bench with wrists hanging off the edge, palms down.
Hold a barbell with an overhand (palms-down) grip.
Let your wrists flex down, lowering the bar.
Extend your wrists upward, raising the bar.
Squeeze the top of your forearms at the peak.
Lower under control.
Keep forearms pinned to the bench — only wrists move.
Use light weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps. Extensors are weaker than flexors.
Builds the forearm extensors
Helps prevent tennis elbow
Balances flexor-to-extensor strength
Easy to load progressively
Important for grip health
Simple setup

musclesWorked: Wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis, extensor carpi ulnaris)

description.en: The bodyweight overhead squat performs a squat with both arms locked out overhead. With no weight, it serves as a mobility assessment and development tool — testing shoulder, thoracic, hip, and ankle mobility simultaneously. It is used by coaches to assess movement quality.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Raise both arms straight overhead, biceps by your ears.
Maintain the overhead arm position throughout.
Squat down while keeping arms overhead.
Descend as deep as your mobility allows.
Keep arms directly above your midfoot — they should not drift forward.
Drive through your feet to stand.
If your arms fall forward, your thoracic or shoulder mobility needs work.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps or use as a mobility assessment.
Tests and develops total-body mobility
Assesses shoulder, thoracic, hip, and ankle mobility
Reveals movement weaknesses
No equipment needed
Useful coaching assessment tool
Progression toward loaded overhead squats

description.en: The bodyweight wood chop squat combines a squat with a diagonal wood chop motion. As you stand up from the squat, you sweep the arms diagonally across the body in a wood chop motion. The combination builds leg strength while training rotational core power, all without equipment.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
Clasp your hands together in front of your chest.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Lower into a squat by sitting your hips back.
As you squat, bring your hands toward the outside of your right foot.
Drive up through your heels to standing.
As you stand, sweep your arms diagonally up across your body.
Finish with arms reaching up and to the left. Alternate sides each rep.
Combines leg work with rotational core
Builds rotational core power
No equipment required
Time-efficient combo movement
Strong oblique engagement
Useful for athletic training

description.en: Butterfly Pose (Baddha Konasana, also called Bound Angle Pose) is a foundational seated yoga pose where you sit with the soles of your feet pressed together and knees dropping out to the sides. It opens the inner thighs, groin, and hips. Adding a forward fold deepens the stretch significantly. It is identical in intent to the seated groin stretch.

en: Sit on the floor with legs extended. Bend both knees and bring the soles of your feet together.
Let your knees drop out to the sides. Pull your heels toward your groin as close as comfortable.
Hold your feet with both hands. Sit up tall with chest lifted.
Press your knees gently toward the floor with your elbows for a deeper stretch.
For more depth, fold forward from the hips with a flat back. Reach your forehead toward your feet.
Hold for 30 to 90 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Avoid forcing your knees down — let gravity do the work over time.
Use a folded blanket or block under each knee for support if needed.
Opens the inner thighs, groin, and hips
Improves hip flexibility for squats and wide-stance lifts
Calming and restorative pose
No equipment needed
Useful for athletes and lifters with tight adductors
Foundational hip-opening yoga pose

description.en: The cable one-arm lateral raise uses a low cable to perform a single-arm lateral raise, targeting the lateral deltoid with constant cable tension. Unlike dumbbells, the cable provides resistance even at the bottom of the movement.

en: Set a cable to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle.
Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your far hand (cable crosses behind your body).
Stand tall. Arm at your side, slight elbow bend.
Raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height.
Squeeze your lateral delt at the top.
Lower under control.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Constant cable tension even at the bottom
Superior to dumbbells for constant tension
Strict unilateral isolation
Easy to load progressively
Builds the lateral delt cap
Reveals left-right imbalances

description.en: The cable press on exercise ball is performed lying back on a stability ball while pressing cable handles forward in a chest press pattern. The unstable ball surface demands strong core and shoulder stabilization on top of the chest pressing work. It builds chest strength with strong stability development.

en: Set both cable pulleys to chest height with single handles.
Position a stability ball between the two cable stations.
Lie back on the ball with your upper back supported.
Grip a handle in each hand at chest level with palms forward.
Plant your feet flat for stability.
Brace your core hard.
Press both handles forward until your arms are fully extended.
Lower the handles back to chest level with control while maintaining ball stability.
Strong stabilization demand
Builds chest, triceps, and shoulders
Develops core stability under press
Useful for athletes who need stability
Different stimulus than bench-supported pressing
Easy to scale by changing cable resistance

description.en: The cable seated shoulder internal rotation is a rotator cuff strengthening exercise where you sit sideways to a cable set at elbow height and rotate your forearm inward across your body. It targets the subscapularis — the internal rotator of the shoulder. It is essential for shoulder health and injury prevention.

en: Set a cable pulley to elbow height. Attach a D-handle.
Sit sideways to the cable with your working arm closest to the cable.
Grip the handle with your working hand. Pin your elbow against your side, forearm pointing toward the cable.
Rotate your forearm inward across your body — away from the cable.
Continue rotating until your forearm is across your stomach.
Slowly let the cable pull your forearm back to the starting position.
Keep your elbow pinned to your side throughout — only your forearm rotates.
Use very light weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side.
Strengthens the subscapularis (internal rotator)
Essential for shoulder health and injury prevention
Constant cable tension throughout rotation
Easy to load progressively with small increments
Critical for overhead athletes and lifters
Rehabilitation and prehabilitation exercise

description.en: The cable unilateral bicep curl is performed standing at a low cable station with a single D-handle. Curling one arm at a time creates focused single-arm bicep work with the constant tension of cables. The unilateral pattern corrects strength imbalances and allows mind-muscle focus on the working bicep.

en: Set a cable to the lowest pulley position with a single D-handle.
Stand facing the cable station with feet shoulder-width apart.
Grip the handle in your right hand with an underhand grip.
Step back slightly to create cable tension with arm extended.
Brace your core and pin your right elbow against your side.
Curl the handle up by bending only at the elbow.
Squeeze your bicep hard at the top.
Lower the handle back down with control to full extension. Complete reps, then switch arms.
Constant cable tension through the range
Single-arm work corrects imbalances
Allows mind-muscle focus on working bicep
Strict form enforced by cable resistance
Builds bicep size and strength
Useful for hypertrophy training

description.en: The dumbbell alternate chest press on stability ball is a chest press performed with the upper back resting on a ball. The lifter presses one dumbbell up at a time while the other stays at the chest. The unstable surface and asymmetrical load force serious core engagement.

en: Sit on a stability ball holding a dumbbell in each hand.
Walk your feet forward and let the upper back roll onto the ball.
Lift your hips so your body forms a flat tabletop.
Press both dumbbells up over your chest with palms facing forward.
Lower one dumbbell down to your chest while the other stays up.
Press the lower dumbbell back up to lockout.
Lower the other dumbbell down and press it back up.
Continue alternating arms with slow control.
Builds chest and triceps
Trains core stability
Recruits stabilizers
Asymmetrical loading challenge
Improves balance
Strong functional move

description.en: The dumbbell bench dip is a weighted version of the bench dip, with a dumbbell placed across your hips for additional resistance. Performing dips between two benches or off a single bench with feet elevated, the added load builds tricep strength far beyond what bodyweight allows.

en: Sit on the edge of a flat bench with hands gripping the edge next to your hips.
Place a dumbbell across your upper thighs and hold it in place.
Extend your legs out in front of you with heels on the floor (or on a second bench for harder).
Slide your hips off the bench so your weight is supported on your hands.
Lower your body by bending your elbows until your upper arms are parallel to the floor.
Keep your elbows tucked rather than flaring out.
Press back up by extending your elbows until arms are straight.
Maintain control of the dumbbell on your hips throughout the set.
Adds heavy load to bench dips for triceps overload
Develops triceps size and strength
Trains the lower chest and front delts as supporting muscles
Easy to set up at any gym
Allows progressive overload beyond bodyweight
Excellent finisher for arm or chest day

description.en: The dumbbell reverse curl is a forearm and brachialis exercise performed with dumbbells held in an overhand (pronated) grip — palms facing the body throughout the curl. The reversed grip shifts emphasis from the biceps brachii to the brachialis and forearm extensors, building visible arm thickness.

en: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Hold them with an overhand grip — palms facing your thighs.
Pin your elbows to your sides. Brace your core.
Curl both dumbbells up by bending at the elbows. Keep the overhand grip throughout.
Continue until the dumbbells reach shoulder height. Squeeze hard at the top.
Lower under control over two seconds.
Use lighter weight than standard curls — the overhand position is significantly harder.
Keep your wrists strong and stable throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Targets the brachialis and forearm extensors
Builds arm thickness that bicep curls miss
Develops forearm strength
Helps prevent tennis elbow
Easy to do at home
Useful balance to bicep-dominant training

description.en: The dumbbell bicep curl squat is a compound combination exercise where you perform a bicep curl at the top of a squat. You hold dumbbells at your sides, squat down, and as you stand, curl the dumbbells to your shoulders. It is a time-efficient full-body exercise that builds arms, legs, and conditioning simultaneously.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms forward.
Squat down by sitting your hips back and bending your knees.
At the bottom of the squat, your arms hang straight with dumbbells near the floor.
Drive through your feet to stand.
As you reach standing, curl both dumbbells up to your shoulders.
Lower the dumbbells back to your sides as you descend into the next squat.
Continue fluidly for the desired reps.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Full-body combination exercise
Builds arms and legs simultaneously
Excellent for conditioning
Time-efficient
Easy to scale by adjusting weight
Engaging variation for circuit training

description.en: The dumbbell farmer's carry is a loaded carry exercise where you walk for distance or time while holding a dumbbell in each hand. It builds grip strength, trap size, core stability, and conditioning all at once — and works at home with a single pair of dumbbells. It is one of the simplest, most effective accessory exercises in any program.

en: Set a pair of heavy dumbbells on the floor. Hinge down and grip them firmly.
Stand up tall by driving through your feet. Pull your shoulders down and back. Keep your chest tall.
Brace your core hard. The dumbbells should hang at arm’s length at your sides.
Begin walking forward with controlled, even steps. Keep your gait normal.
Maintain perfect posture throughout. Do not let the dumbbells pull your shoulders forward or rotate your torso.
Walk for the prescribed distance (e.g., 50 to 100 feet) or time (e.g., 30 to 60 seconds).
At the finish, set the dumbbells down with a controlled hip-hinge — not by dropping them or rounding your back.
Use straps for very heavy loading if grip is the limiting factor.
Builds grip strength effectively with home equipment
Develops the upper traps, forearms, and core simultaneously
Trains posture and shoulder stability under load
Easy to scale up by using heavier dumbbells
Excellent finisher for any workout
Carries over directly to real-life loaded carrying tasks

description.en: The dumbbell good morning is a hip-hinge exercise performed holding a dumbbell at your chest or behind your neck while bowing forward at the hips. It trains the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back. It is more accessible than the barbell good morning and a useful at-home posterior chain exercise.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold a dumbbell at your chest with both hands (goblet position).
Set a slight, fixed bend in your knees. Brace your core.
Hinge forward at the hips by pushing your butt back. Keep your back flat throughout.
Lower your torso until it is roughly parallel to the floor (or wherever you feel a strong hamstring stretch).
Drive your hips forward to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Keep the dumbbell pressed against your chest the entire time.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Use moderate weight. Form matters more than load on this exercise.
Trains the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back
Reinforces the hip-hinge pattern
More accessible than barbell good mornings
Easier on the back than barbell variations
Works at home with one dumbbell
Excellent posterior chain accessory

description.en: The dumbbell lying alternate extension performs the lying tricep extension (skull crusher pattern) one arm at a time. While one dumbbell stays extended over the chest, the working arm lowers behind the head and presses back up. The alternating pattern increases time under tension and corrects strength imbalances.

en: Lie on a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand pressed over your chest.
Hold both dumbbells with palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Start with both arms extended over the chest.
Brace your core and pin your shoulders to the bench.
Lower the right dumbbell behind your head by bending only at the elbow.
Keep the left arm fully extended over the chest throughout.
Press the right dumbbell back up to the starting position.
Repeat with the left arm, alternating sides each rep.
Single-arm tricep work corrects imbalances
Increases time under tension on each side
Adds core anti-rotation challenge
Builds tricep size and strength
Useful for breaking through tricep plateaus
Strict form on each side

description.en: The dumbbell one arm decline chest press performs the decline dumbbell press one arm at a time. While one hand rests at the side, the working arm presses with full range. Single-arm work emphasizes the lower chest while the off-arm position adds a strong core anti-rotation challenge.

en: Set a bench to a decline angle and secure your feet on the foot pads.
Lie back with a single dumbbell in your right hand.
Press the dumbbell up over your chest with arm extended.
Place your left hand at your side or on your stomach.
Brace your core hard to resist rotation.
Lower the dumbbell down to your chest with control.
Press the dumbbell back up to the starting position.
Complete reps on one side, then switch arms.
Targets lower chest unilaterally
Strong anti-rotation core challenge
Corrects chest strength imbalances
Builds chest size and strength
Useful for athletic carryover
Different stimulus than two-arm press

description.en: The dumbbell seated kickback performs tricep kickbacks while seated on the end of a bench, hinging forward at the hips. The seated position provides stability and eliminates lower back fatigue that can limit standing kickbacks on high-rep sets.

en: Sit on the end of a flat bench. Hold a dumbbell in each hand.
Hinge forward at the hips so your chest is close to your thighs.
Pin your upper arms against your sides, elbows at 90 degrees.
Extend both forearms straight back by straightening at the elbows.
Lock out. Squeeze your triceps at the top.
Slowly bend your elbows back to 90 degrees.
Keep upper arms still throughout.
Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Seated position provides stability
Eliminates lower back fatigue
Strict tricep isolation
Peak contraction at lockout
Useful for high-rep sets
Simple setup

description.en: The dumbbell seated one arm rotate is a Russian twist style move where one dumbbell is held and twisted side to side from a seated V position. The single-arm pattern challenges anti-rotation on the empty side while building rotational power on the working side. It is a strong core developer.

en: Sit on the floor with knees bent and feet lifted off the ground.
Lean back slightly to create a V shape with your torso and thighs.
Hold a single dumbbell in both hands at chest level.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Rotate the torso to twist the dumbbell to one side of the body.
Tap the dumbbell to the floor next to your hip.
Twist back through the center to the other side.
Continue rotating side to side with control.
Builds rotational core strength
Hits the obliques hard
Trains anti-rotation control
Improves trunk power
Useful for athletes
Brutal core finisher

description.en: The exercise ball alternating arm ups is a core stability drill done in a forearm plank with the elbows on a ball. Lifting one arm overhead at a time forces the core to anti-rotate while the shoulders stabilize.

en: Set up in a forearm plank with both elbows on a stability ball.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace the core hard and squeeze the glutes.
Keep the hips level and square to the floor.
Lift one arm forward off the ball and reach up.
Hold the arm overhead briefly.
Lower with control to the start.
Alternate arms for the working set.
Trains the core for anti-rotation.
Builds shoulder stability.
Stability ball adds challenge.
Useful for athletic carryover.
Improves total body control.

description.en: The floor fly with towels is a sliding chest fly using small towels on a smooth floor. The lifter starts in a high plank with hands on towels, then slides the hands out wide and back together. The sliding motion creates a brutal chest fly with bodyweight.

en: Place a small towel under each hand on a smooth floor.
Begin in a high plank position with hands under shoulders.
Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line.
Slide both hands out wide to the sides at the same time.
Continue sliding until the chest lowers toward the floor.
Stop with the arms in a wide fly position.
Squeeze the chest to slide the hands back together.
Return to the start at the top.
Brutal chest builder
No equipment beyond towels
Trains core stability
Builds the chest
Useful chest builder
Easy at-home setup

description.en: The lever good morning on the hack squat machine uses the hack squat platform with the shoulder pads loaded across the upper traps. Hinging at the hips trains the posterior chain with a fixed and supported path.

en: Set up under a hack squat machine with the shoulder pads on your traps.
Plant the feet shoulder width on the platform.
Stand up tall to unrack the weight.
Brace the core and set the back flat.
Hinge at the hips by pushing the hips back.
Allow a slight bend in the knees and lower the torso.
Stop when the torso is roughly parallel to the floor or hamstring tension caps the range.
Drive the hips forward to stand back tall and repeat.
Builds hamstring and erector strength under a fixed path.
Hack squat support reduces balance demands compared to barbell good mornings.
Carryover to deadlifts and squats.
Trains the hip hinge under load.
Easier to load heavy than free weight versions.
Saves the spine from bar pressure on the neck.

description.en: The hip roll plank starts in a forearm plank and rolls to a side plank on one side, returns to front plank, then rolls to the other side. It trains the core through all angles — anti-extension in the front plank and anti-lateral flexion in the side planks.

en: Start in a forearm plank.
Rotate to a side plank on your right forearm. Stack or stagger your feet.
Hold the side plank for 1 to 2 seconds.
Rotate back to front plank.
Rotate to a side plank on your left forearm.
Continue rolling front → right → front → left.
Maintain body alignment through each position.
Aim for 5 to 8 rolls per side.
Trains the core through all angles
Combines front and side plank demands
Builds anti-extension and anti-lateral flexion
No equipment needed
Develops rotational transitions
Engaging dynamic plank variation

description.en: The jack knife sit-up (also called the V-up) is a core exercise where you lie on your back and simultaneously lift your torso and legs to meet in a V-shape, with your hands reaching toward your toes. It trains both the upper and lower abs in one movement and is a more advanced version of the standard sit-up.

en: Lie flat on your back with arms extended overhead and legs straight.
Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor.
Simultaneously lift your torso and your straight legs upward, reaching your hands toward your feet.
Meet at the top in a V-shape with your fingers reaching toward your toes.
Squeeze your abs hard at the top.
Lower under control back to the start with arms overhead and legs extended.
Stop just before your hands and heels touch the floor to maintain tension.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use bent knees if too difficult.
Trains upper and lower abs simultaneously
Builds core strength and endurance
No equipment needed
Time-efficient core exercise
Excellent finisher for ab workouts
Develops body control

description.en: The jack plank (also known as the plank jack) is a dynamic plank variation where you hold a high plank position while jumping your feet apart and back together — like a jumping jack with the upper body in a plank. It builds core stability, shoulder endurance, and provides cardio.

en: Get into a high plank position with hands shoulder-width apart, body in a straight line from heels to head.
Brace your core hard. Keep your hips stable.
Jump both feet out wider than your hips simultaneously.
Immediately jump both feet back together to the start position.
Continue jumping your feet in and out rapidly.
Maintain the plank position throughout — only your legs move.
Do not let your hips bounce up and down or sag toward the floor.
Perform for 20 to 45 seconds per set.
Builds core stability with cardio demand
Develops shoulder endurance
Excellent HIIT exercise
Trains hip stability under movement
No equipment needed
Time-efficient core/cardio combo

description.en: The kettlebell single-arm clean and press is a full-body compound lift combining a single-arm clean (explosive pull to the front rack) with an overhead press. It builds total-body strength, power, and conditioning with one kettlebell. It is a foundational kettlebell sport event.

en: Place a kettlebell on the floor. Hinge down and grip with one hand.
Hike the bell back and clean it to the front-rack position using hip drive.
Stand tall with the bell at your shoulder. Brace your core.
Press the bell straight overhead until your arm is locked out.
Lower the bell back to the rack, then swing it back between your legs for the next clean.
Each rep is: clean → rack → press → lower → swing back → repeat.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
Keep the movement rhythmic and flowing.
Full-body strength and power in one movement
Builds explosive hip drive and pressing strength
Excellent conditioning exercise
Foundational kettlebell sport event
Trains grip, core, and shoulders heavily
Needs only one kettlebell

description.en: The kettlebell standing slingshots, also called body passes or halos, involve passing a kettlebell around your body in a horizontal circle. With the kettlebell held in front, you swing it around behind you and back to the front. The continuous circular motion trains shoulder mobility, core stability, and grip strength.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a kettlebell in your right hand at hip level.
Brace your core hard.
Pass the kettlebell behind your back to your left hand.
Catch the kettlebell with your left hand behind your back.
Bring the kettlebell around the front to your right hand.
Catch with your right hand and continue the circular motion.
Keep the kettlebell moving in a smooth circular path around your body.
Reverse direction partway through the set.
Trains shoulder mobility
Builds core stability through rotation
Develops grip strength and hand control
No setup required beyond a kettlebell
Useful as warm-up or finisher
Strong functional movement pattern

description.en: The lying T spine mobility stretch is a side lying open book variation. With the knees stacked and rotating the top arm across the body, you mobilize the thoracic spine through rotation.

en: Lie on your side with the knees stacked and bent at ninety degrees.
Stretch both arms out in front of you in a stack.
Brace the core and keep the knees pinned together.
Rotate the top arm up and across the body to the other side.
Follow the moving hand with your eyes.
Open the chest as the arm reaches the floor on the opposite side.
Pause briefly and feel the stretch through the upper back.
Return to the start and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Improves thoracic spine rotational mobility.
Opens the chest and shoulders.
Reduces upper back stiffness.
Carryover to better squat and overhead positions.
Excellent warm up before lifting.
No equipment needed.

description.en: The lever seated right side crunch is an oblique builder performed on a seated ab crunch machine angled for one side. The lifter sits and crunches the torso to the right, loading the right obliques against the lever resistance. The machine isolates the obliques.

en: Sit on a lever ab crunch machine with the resistance set.
Position the body so the right side faces the lever.
Grip the handles and set the chest pad against the torso.
Brace your core and set the feet under the foot pads.
Crunch the torso to the right bending sideways.
Squeeze the right obliques hard at the bottom.
Hold briefly at the contracted position.
Return to the start with control. Complete reps.
Strong oblique isolation
Constant lever resistance
Easy to scale loading
Builds the obliques
Useful core builder
Strong machine move

description.en: The medicine ball supine chest throw is an explosive pressing exercise where you lie on your back, hold a medicine ball at your chest, and throw it straight up as high as possible. It develops explosive pressing power without deceleration — unlike a bench press, you release the ball at the top for maximum velocity.

en: Lie on your back on the floor or a flat bench. Hold a medicine ball at your chest with both hands.
Brace your core. Press your back flat.
Explosively press and release the ball straight up as high as possible.
Catch the ball as it comes back down. Absorb the catch by letting it return to your chest.
Immediately throw it up again.
Use a non-bouncing medicine ball (dead ball) if throwing alone to avoid dangerous rebounds.
A partner can catch and return the ball from above.
Aim for 8 to 12 throws per set with maximum effort each rep.
Develops explosive pressing power
No deceleration phase — maximum velocity
Carries over to bench press explosiveness
Builds fast-twitch fiber recruitment
Simple execution
Excellent for athletes

description.en: The neck flexor stretch is a simple stretch where you gently tilt your head backward to look up, stretching the front of the neck (sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles). It counteracts the forward head posture caused by screen time and helps relieve front-neck tightness.

en: Sit or stand tall with shoulders pulled back and down.
Slowly tilt your head backward, looking up toward the ceiling.
Allow your jaw to relax and your mouth to open slightly.
Feel the stretch through the front of your neck and throat.
Hold for 15 to 20 seconds. Breathe normally.
Slowly return your head to neutral position.
Repeat 2 to 3 times.
Move slowly and never force the stretch — protect your cervical spine.
Stretches the front of the neck
Counteracts forward head posture
Quick and accessible
No equipment needed
Useful for desk workers
Improves cervical spine mobility

description.en: The push-up on a Bosu ball is a push-up variation where your hands grip the rounded side of a Bosu ball (flat side down) during the push-up. The unstable surface dramatically increases stabilizer engagement, especially in the rotator cuff and core. It is an advanced push-up variation.

en: Place a Bosu ball on the floor with the flat side down (rounded side up).
Grip the sides of the rounded surface with both hands.
Walk your feet back into a high plank position with hands on the Bosu.
Brace your core hard. Form a straight body line from heels to head.
Lower your chest toward the Bosu by bending at the elbows.
Lower until your chest is just above the Bosu.
Press back up to lockout, controlling the unstable surface throughout.
Maintain straight body line. The Bosu will wobble — control it with strong stabilizers.
Heavy stabilizer engagement from instability
Builds rotator cuff stability
Demands strong core engagement
Develops shoulder stability under load
Engaging push-up variation
Useful for athletes

description.en: The resistance band squat with single arm row is a combo exercise where a band-loaded squat is performed and a single-arm row is added at the top of each rep. The result is a full-body move that hits the legs and back together for an efficient training stimulus.

en: Stand on a resistance band with feet at shoulder-width.
Hold each end of the band with arms hanging down.
Bend down into a squat with the chest up and knees tracking the toes.
Drive through the heels to stand up to full lockout.
At the top, row one end of the band to your ribs by pulling the elbow back.
Squeeze the back muscles at the top of the row.
Lower the band back down and reset.
Squat back down to start. Alternate the rowing arm each rep.
Trains legs and back together
Combo move saves time
Builds full-body strength
Constant band tension
Travel-friendly equipment
Useful conditioning combo

description.en: The resistance band standing front warming up is a light activation drill done before pressing work. Pressing a band forward at chest height warms up the front delts and chest in a primed pressing pattern.

en: Anchor a resistance band behind you at chest height.
Stand facing away from the anchor.
Grab the band with both hands at chest level.
Step forward to create tension.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Press both hands forward to extend the arms.
Squeeze the front delts and chest at full extension.
Return to the start and continue for the working set.
Warms up the front delts.
Activates the chest.
Useful pre-workout.
Improves shoulder health.
Builds pressing readiness.

description.en: The ring chest fly is a bodyweight chest fly performed on gymnastic rings. You face away from the ring anchor and arc your arms wide in a fly motion, then bring them back together. The rings provide greater instability than TRX straps, demanding more shoulder stability and core engagement.

en: Set gymnastic rings to chest height. Face away from the anchor.
Grip the rings. Step back into a forward-leaning plank position.
Start with arms extended forward, palms facing inward.
Arc both arms out to the sides in a wide fly motion. Maintain slight elbow bend.
Lower your chest between the rings for a deep stretch.
Pull the rings back together by squeezing your chest.
Maintain straight body line throughout.
More horizontal body angle is harder. Use slow, controlled movement.
Greater instability than TRX for max stabilizer demand
Deep chest stretch at the bottom
Constant bodyweight tension
Builds elite shoulder stability
Scalable by adjusting body angle
No bench needed

description.en: The roll ball forearm supinator is a self myofascial release drill for the supinator at the outer elbow. Pressing a ball into the supinator releases tightness that contributes to lateral elbow pain.

en: Sit at a table with one forearm resting on top palm down.
Place a massage ball just below the outer elbow.
Press the forearm down into the ball.
Use the other hand to add pressure.
Roll the upper outer forearm slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Stay near the elbow rather than the wrist.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the supinator.
Reduces outer elbow tightness.
Improves forearm rotation.
Useful for racquet sports.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The roll ball lying semispinalis capitis muscle activation is a self myofascial release drill for the deep neck extensors. A small ball pressed at the base of the skull while lying down releases the semispinalis capitis and reduces tension related headaches.

en: Lie on the back on the floor.
Place a small massage ball at the base of the skull off to one side.
Bend the knees with feet flat for stability.
Brace the core and keep the body relaxed.
Allow the head to settle onto the ball.
Tip the head gently to deepen the pressure.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the deep neck extensors.
Reduces tension headaches.
Improves neck mobility.
Useful for desk workers.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The seated lower back stretch is a gentle stretch performed sitting in a chair where you fold forward and let your torso hang down between your knees. The position uses gravity to decompress the lower back and stretch the entire spine. It is one of the simplest stretches for relieving back tension at work or home.

en: Sit on the edge of a chair with feet flat on the floor, slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Sit up tall with chest lifted.
Slowly fold forward at the hips, letting your torso drop between your knees.
Let your arms hang toward the floor or rest on your shins.
Let your head hang heavy. Allow gravity to decompress your spine.
Feel the gentle stretch through your lower back and posterior chain.
Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Slowly roll up to seated, vertebra by vertebra.
Decompresses the lower back gently
Stretches the entire spine
Practical for office settings
No equipment needed beyond a chair
Relieves daily back tension
Calming and grounding

description.en: The standing toe-up calf stretch is a simple standing stretch where you place the ball of your foot against a wall or step and lean forward to stretch the calf. It targets the gastrocnemius primarily and is one of the quickest, most accessible calf stretches available.

en: Stand facing a wall or step. Place the ball of your right foot against the wall or on the edge of the step, with the heel on the floor.
Keep your right knee straight. Lean your body forward by shifting your hips toward the wall.
Feel the stretch through your right calf muscle.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply and relax into the stretch.
For a deeper stretch, lean further forward or step closer to the wall.
Switch to the left foot and repeat.
To bias the soleus, perform the same stretch with a slightly bent knee.
Perform two to three sets per side as needed.
Quick, accessible calf stretch that works anywhere
Targets the gastrocnemius effectively
Improves ankle dorsiflexion for better squat depth
Relieves calf tightness from running or high heels
Excellent warm-up or cool-down stretch
No equipment needed

description.en: The standing ab wheel rollout is the most advanced version of the ab wheel rollout — performed from the feet instead of the knees. The increased lever arm makes it exponentially harder than the kneeling version. It is one of the hardest core exercises in existence and demands elite anti-extension strength.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding an ab wheel on the floor in front of your toes.
Bend at the hips to reach the wheel. Grip the handles.
Brace your core extremely hard. Tuck your pelvis (posterior tilt).
Slowly roll the wheel forward, extending your body.
Continue rolling until your body is nearly horizontal — arms overhead, body straight.
Do NOT let your lower back arch at any point. If it arches, you have gone too far.
Pull yourself back to standing by contracting your abs and lats.
Master the kneeling rollout for sets of 15+ before attempting standing.
One of the hardest core exercises in existence
Builds elite anti-extension strength
Develops lat and shoulder strength
Benchmark calisthenics core exercise
No equipment needed besides an ab wheel
Progresses from kneeling rollouts

description.en: The straight-leg sit-up performs a sit-up with legs fully extended on the floor rather than bent. The straight legs increase hip flexor involvement and make the sit-up harder by lengthening the lever arm.

en: Lie on your back with legs fully extended, feet on the floor. Arms across chest or behind head.
Anchor your feet under something heavy or have a partner hold them.
Sit up fully by flexing your spine and hips.
The straight legs make this harder than bent-knee sit-ups.
Lower under control.
If you cannot sit up with straight legs, bend them slightly.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
This involves more hip flexor than bent-knee versions.
Increased difficulty from straight legs
Builds hip flexor and ab strength together
No equipment needed
Challenging sit-up variation
Greater range of motion
Tests core and hip flexor strength

description.en: The strongman wheelbarrow is a loaded carry event where you lift and walk with a weighted wheelbarrow-style implement. You grip the handles, lift, and walk for distance. It builds full-body strength, grip endurance, and leg drive.

en: Stand behind a loaded wheelbarrow implement. Grip both handles firmly.
Brace your core. Lift the handles by driving through your legs.
Stand tall with the wheelbarrow balanced on its wheel.
Walk forward with controlled strides.
Maintain upright posture. Steer the wheelbarrow straight.
Walk for the desired distance as fast as possible.
Set down carefully at the end.
This is a strongman competition event — practice with moderate weight first.
Full-body strength and conditioning
Builds grip endurance
Develops leg drive and walking power
Strongman competition event
Builds mental toughness
Unique implement training

description.en: The suspender middle row is a TRX inverted row variation that emphasizes the middle back. The pulling path is to the lower chest with elbows tucked closer to the body. The position targets the rhomboids and middle traps more directly than the standard inverted row.

en: Adjust suspension straps to about waist height.
Grip the handles with palms facing each other (neutral grip).
Walk your feet forward until you are leaning back.
Position your body in a straight line.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes.
Pull your body up to the handles, bringing them to your lower chest.
Keep elbows tucked closer to the body during the pull.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together hard, then lower with control.
Targets middle back and rhomboids
Builds back strength with bodyweight
Strong rhomboid engagement
No weights required
Different stimulus than standard inverted row
Useful for posture work

description.en: The suspender self assisted triceps dip is a TRX dip variation with an upright torso to bias the triceps. The lifter dips between the handles with feet on the floor for assistance. It is a useful tricep builder.

en: Set the suspension trainer to elbow height.
Grip the handles with palms facing inward.
Keep the torso upright throughout.
Step the feet forward for assistance.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Lower the body by bending the elbows.
Keep the elbows tight to the sides.
Press back up to lockout by extending the triceps.
Trains the triceps
Strong dip variation
Builds the upper arms
Adjustable assistance
Useful tricep builder

description.en: The suspension trainer alternate superman is an advanced TRX core and chest move. The lifter holds a TRX push-up plank position and reaches one handle forward at a time into a long superman extension. The alternating reaches build extreme core and shoulder strength.

en: Set a suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip the handles and step back to a plank.
Brace your core hard and keep the body in a straight line.
Reach one handle forward in a long arm extension.
Hold the superman reach briefly.
Pull the handle back to the start.
Reach the other handle forward.
Continue alternating reaches with control.
Advanced TRX move
Builds shoulder stability
Trains core anti-extension
Strong functional builder
Brutal core challenge
Useful TRX exercise

description.en: The wide grip pull-up is a vertical pulling exercise performed by hanging from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip wider than shoulder-width and pulling your body up. The wide grip shifts emphasis to the upper lats and teres major, building serious back width and the foundation of a V-taper. It is harder than a standard pull-up due to the reduced bicep involvement.

en: Reach up and grip a sturdy pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands roughly 1.5 times shoulder-width apart.
Wrap your thumbs around the bar. Hang with arms fully extended, feet off the floor.
Pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position. Brace your core.
Pull your body up by driving your elbows down and out toward your hips. Lead with your chest.
Aim to bring your upper chest to bar level. Squeeze your lats hard at the top.
Lower yourself slowly under control to a full hang with arms completely straight.
Avoid kipping or swinging. Strict reps are far more valuable than partial sloppy reps.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Add weight via a dip belt as you get stronger.
Builds the upper lats and back width more than narrow-grip variations
Develops the V-taper look
Trains the lats with reduced bicep involvement
Builds grip strength and shoulder stability
Highly portable — needs only a pull-up bar
Excellent benchmark for upper-body strength
